vignette: Leila, a 22-year-old South Eastern Asian woman, had always been proud of her independence. As a call center agent, she was confident in her ability to handle high-pressure situations and provide excellent customer service. However, it was on one fateful night, about six months ago, that Leila's life took a drastic turn. She was sexually assaulted by an acquaintance while walking home from work. The experience left her feeling shattered and helpless. The days following the assault were a blur for Leila. She struggled to recall specific details of the event, but fragments kept resurfacing in her mind like disconnected puzzle pieces. She remembered the sound of sirens blaring in the distance as she lay frozen on the ground, the metallic taste of blood in her mouth, and the feeling of being trapped with no escape. These memories felt more real to Leila than any ordinary recollection, and they haunted her every waking moment. As time passed, Leila began to notice that certain situations triggered intense anxiety and fear responses within her. The sound of ambulances racing down the street would send her heart racing, transporting her back to that fateful night. Even seeing happy families laughing together on social media or in public places made her feel uneasy, serving as a harsh reminder of all she had lost. Leila's coping mechanisms only seemed to exacerbate her distress. She started avoiding reminders of the event by pushing away supportive friends and family members who tried to talk about it with her. Her husband, once her rock, began to feel like an outsider in their relationship as Leila withdrew from intimate conversations and physical affection. Leila turned to sexual fantasies and activities as a way to release tension, but this coping strategy only left her feeling more disconnected from herself and others. Her job at the call center became increasingly challenging as well. Leila found herself scanning exits whenever she entered the building or a meeting room, constantly on the lookout for potential threats. She would jump in response to unexpected movements nearby, apologizing profusely to coworkers who seemed puzzled by her behavior. Her supervisor's friendly smile now made her feel uneasy, and she went out of her way to avoid interacting with anyone in authority. Leila's hypervigilance extended far beyond the confines of her workplace or home. She would constantly scan her surroundings for signs of danger, whether walking down the street or sitting in a park. Her mind was perpetually on high alert, and she couldn't shake off the feeling that something terrible was waiting to happen. The weight of these experiences has taken its toll on Leila's self-perception. She has come to believe that if she allows herself to think about the assault, she will crumble under the emotional burden. This fear drives her avoidance behaviors, which in turn reinforce her sense of inadequacy. As a result, Leila feels like she is living in a state of perpetual limbo, unsure of how to break free from this cycle of trauma and anxiety. It was only when Leila's husband expressed concerns about the strain their relationship was under that she realized she needed help. She hopes that therapy will provide her with tools to manage her symptoms and rebuild her sense of self-worth. As she takes this first tentative step towards healing, Leila is most afraid that confronting her trauma head-on will be too overwhelming, while simultaneously hoping that she can learn to navigate the world without constantly feeling like she's walking on eggshells.
